content: To effectively implement the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, it is essential to connect individuals with its purpose and directly request their involvement. Every person whose role intersects with the checklist, particularly those working in the operating room (OR), should be engaged in one-on-one conversations before they begin using it. Promoting the checklist within the facility is also vital to create awareness, spark curiosity, and reinforce the shared mission of improving surgical safety. This can be achieved through various forms of internal publicity, such as demonstration videos, bulletin boards, badges, emails, storytelling, and newsletters. However, these promotional efforts should complement, not replace, the one-on-one conversations. Once surgical team members are introduced to the checklist and its benefits, they must be trained to use it effectively before applying it in patient care. Training should include explanations, demonstrations, and opportunities for practice outside the OR. Coaching is the next step in the learning process, following one-on-one conversations and hands-on training. Coaching is essential for successful implementation, as it helps individuals and teams improve performance and sustain effective checklist use over time. Sustaining and improving the checklist's use over time presents a new challenge. It is crucial to maintain focus on the checklist work, even as attention shifts to other priorities. This can be achieved by continually engaging surgical team members through observation, coaching, collecting stories, and conducting annual culture surveys. An implementation team should oversee the project, with periodic changes in team members and updates to the checklist content to meet the organization’s evolving needs. Preventing surgical site infections (SSIs) requires the integration of evidence-based recommendations into daily care. Overburdened health facilities often view quality improvement initiatives as luxuries due to resource constraints. Governments may lack the resources to support checklist implementation fully, often providing materials without accompanying training or support. In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), facilities may display the checklist but fail to use it effectively. Emphasizing implementation without requiring new resources is critical, as most checklist items rely on existing human resources and processes. The checklist serves as a template for all surgical settings, prompting teams to discuss plans, address concerns, verify critical information, and confirm the completion of essential processes. Implementation can begin with parts of the checklist, focusing on addressing gaps and gradually moving toward full adoption. For example, some facilities may start by implementing one section or a single checklist item. Bringing the checklist to LMICs presents unique challenges in dissemination, adoption, and implementation. Limited communication channels and resources often hinder progress. Partnering with ministries of health, non-profits, charities, and professional societies can facilitate dissemination. Strong clinical champions, who help design and test the checklist, are instrumental in its spread and adoption. In LMICs, the checklist's success often depends on adapting workflows to local contexts. For instance, ensuring antibiotics are administered within one hour of incision may require changes in how and where they are provided. The WHO’s multimodal strategy, which includes system changes, education, awareness-raising, evaluation, and feedback, is essential for fostering a safety culture and improving compliance with standards. The Clean Cut program, developed by Lifebox, focuses on preventing SSIs by embedding infection prevention and control (IPC) processes into basic surgical principles. It uses the checklist to engage clinical teams, monitor data, and align practices with standards. The program targets six perioperative standards, such as skin preparation, sterile field maintenance, instrument sterility, antibiotic timing, surgical swab tracking, and verbal time-outs before incision. By mapping upstream steps for each standard, the program identifies barriers and develops contextually relevant solutions. Strong champions and external support are critical for successful and sustained adoption of the checklist in LMICs. Incremental steps, such as implementing one section or item, can help facilities progress toward full implementation. The checklist’s implementation process fosters system change, engages physicians in quality improvement, and promotes a culture of continuous improvement. Key lessons from the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist include the importance of early dissemination strategies, simplicity in design, and multidisciplinary teams. Clinical champions play a vital role in spreading the work, and education should focus on the rationale and goals of patient care changes. Training should be intensive and tailored to the clinical process, with a mix of teaching modalities to reinforce learning. Execution involves designing an SSI intervention toolkit that addresses barriers, standardizes processes, and incorporates independent checks. Local ownership and adaptation to clinical workflows are essential for success. Assigning clear responsibilities, reviewing strategies, and employing specialized professionals can further enhance implementation. Education and training are critical components but must be part of a broader strategy to achieve sustained improvement.
